::: {.hero-section}

This course develops the mathematics used in machine learning: floating-point computation, linear algebra, multivariate calculus and automatic differentiation, probability and estimation, optimization, information theory, and Markov chains. It comprises 26 lectures and 13 tutorials; each meeting is 80 minutes.

The usual order is concrete example, calculation, geometric or probabilistic interpretation, and then the general statement. No prior machine-learning course is assumed. The final two lectures use a character-level language model to connect the main ideas.

:::

## How to use this site
The schedule below links each lecture to its handout PDF and assigned reading. Every second lecture or so is followed by a tutorial with a pen-and-paper worksheet and an executed Jupyter notebook. Supplementary books, notes, videos, and interactive material are collected under [Resources](resources.qmd).
:::

---

## Primary texts and references

The primary text is **Deisenroth, Faisal & Ong, *Mathematics for Machine Learning***. Boyd & Vandenberghe is used for optimization, MacKay for information theory, and Solomon for numerical computation.

| Role | Resource |
|------|----------|
| **Primary** — assigned reading | [Deisenroth et al., *Mathematics for Machine Learning*](https://mml-book.github.io/) — free PDF |
| **Optimization** | [Boyd & Vandenberghe, *Convex Optimization*](https://stanford.edu/~boyd/cvxbook/) — free PDF |
| **Information theory** | [MacKay, *Information Theory, Inference and Learning Algorithms*](https://www.inference.org.uk/itprnn/book.pdf) — free PDF + [video lectures](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLruBu5BI5n4aFpG32iMbdWoRVAA-Vcso6) |
| **Numerics** | [Solomon, *Numerical Algorithms*](https://people.csail.mit.edu/jsolomon/share/book/numerical_book.pdf) — free PDF |
| **Visual intuition** | 3Blue1Brown, [Essence of Linear Algebra](https://www.3blue1brown.com/topics/linear-algebra) · [Essence of Calculus](https://www.3blue1brown.com/topics/calculus) |

## A recurring example

Several lectures revisit a character-level language model:

**L2** log-space computation → **L5/L25** transition matrices and stationary eigenvectors → **L11** gradients through the loss → **L14** maximum-likelihood fitting → **L17** numerical optimization → **L24** cross-entropy and perplexity → **L26** training, evaluation, and sampling.
